html:
In the 10th century huge amounts of Islamic silver coins, most of them minted by the Samanids of Central Asia, flowed north up the Volga river to Scandinavia and the Baltic.

The Samanids ruled from Bukhara and controlled rich silver mines in the mountains of Central Asia. They struck silver dirhams in Samarkand, Tashkent and other cities. Traders carried the coins north to the markets of the Volga Bulgars and the Khazars.

There they met the Rus, Scandinavian traders and raiders who had come down the rivers from the Baltic. The Rus sold furs, wax, honey and slaves, many captured from Slav lands, and took silver home. The Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan saw such Rus traders on the Volga in 922.

The coins turn up in hoards across Russia, Poland and Sweden, above all on the island of Gotland, where tens of thousands have been found. In Scandinavia silver was weighed rather than counted, so many coins are cut into pieces.

The flow dried up around the end of the century, perhaps as the Central Asian mines ran low and the Samanids fell. The trade helped build the towns of Kievan Rus'.
sum: In the 10th century huge amounts of Islamic silver coins, most of them minted by the Samanids of Central Asia, flowed north up the Volga river to Scandinavia and the Baltic.
